screens.title: Developing CorDapps on R3 Corda
screens.subtitle: States, Contracts, Flows — build private, legally-aware distributed applications

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn how CorDapps turn business ideas into executable, privacy-preserving processes on a Corda network. We focus on the three essential parts: immutable data models called ContractState, Contract logic that enforces business rules through a verify function, and FlowLogic that orchestrates multi-party transactions with TransactionBuilder, signature collection, and notarization. You will see concrete Kotlin examples for a DealState data model, a DealContract with Create, Accept, and Settle rules, and an end-to-end CreateDealFlow with a responder. Understanding these parts matters because Corda separates agreement, validation, and execution, giving you strong privacy controls and legal clarity. For example, a lender and borrower can exchange a DealState that only those participants can see, while the contract ensures status transitions are valid before signatures are applied. A common misconception is that notarization equals validation — in Corda, the contract. verify checks correctness before parties sign, and the Notary only prevents double-spend. As you move through the lesson you’ll practice mapping a business rule to a verify assertion, writing a flow that collects signatures, and packaging a CorDapp JAR for deployment. Ready to dive into states, contracts and flows with practical Kotlin examples?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Design immutable states, enforce rules with Contract.verify, and implement multi-step Flows to build CorDapps that record shared facts privately and correctly.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will be able to demonstrate after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to design ContractState objects that represent assets or agreements, write Contract. verify functions that enforce transitions, and implement FlowLogic to orchestrate multi-party transactions. First, you will design and implement ContractState objects so that each state includes the right fields and participant list. A concrete example is creating a DealState containing dealId, value, lender, borrower, and status. Second, you will develop Contract logic with a verify function that throws on violations; for instance, requiring that a created deal has a positive value and different lender and borrower. Third, you will construct flows that build transactions with TransactionBuilder, collect signatures using CollectSignaturesFlow, and finalize via FinalityFlow and a Notary. Finally, you will understand how to build and deploy a CorDapp JAR to node cordapps folders for testing and production. A common misconception is that the Notary validates business rules; in Corda, parties run verify locally before signing. Practice these objectives by inspecting the example DealContract and flows, and consider how participants affect privacy and distribution.

screens.title: States: ContractState explained
screens.subtitle: Immutable ledger facts and participant visibility

narration.text: A ContractState is an immutable data structure that represents a fact, asset, or agreement on the Corda ledger at a specific moment. It declares the fields that describe the fact and a participants list that controls who receives and can sign transactions involving that state. Immutability means you never modify a state in place; instead, a transaction consumes the existing state as an input and creates a new output state representing the updated fact. For example, a DealState with a status field moves from PROPOSED to ACCEPTED by consuming the PROPOSED input and producing an ACCEPTED output. A common misconception is treating states like mutable database rows; in Corda they are historical snapshots and every change must be recorded as a new state. Practically, participants are crucial: if a party is not included in participants, they will not receive transaction proposals or be able to sign, which often causes missing-transaction errors. When designing a state, think carefully about which parties must see the data and which fields need to be included for contract verification. Key takeaway: states model the shared facts, and their participants control distribution and privacy. How would you design participants for a three-party deal where an observer should see but not sign?

keyIdea.title: State rule
keyIdea.text: Model facts immutably and include all parties that must receive or sign related transactions in participants.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › States: ContractState explained
Definition
A ContractState records a fact; it is immutable and includes a participants list that determines distribution and signing rights.
Explanation bullets
  • Immutable snapshot: updates create new output states while inputs are consumed.
  • Participants list defines who receives the transaction and can sign—missing participants cause distribution issues.
  • States are linked to a governing contract via @BelongsToContract for verification.
Key Takeaway

Design states as immutable facts; list every party that must see or sign the data.

Concrete example
DealState models a loan-like agreement. It includes dealId, value, lender, borrower, status, and participants. The participants list includes lender and borrower so both receive related transactions.
// fields shown for clarity
data class DealState(
  val dealId: String,
  val value: Long,
  val lender: Party,
  val borrower: Party,
  val status: String,
  override val participants: List<Party>
) : ContractState
Misconception: States are not mutable records. Changing status requires a transaction that consumes the old state and creates a new one.

screens.title: DealState Kotlin example
screens.subtitle: Walk through the data structure and annotations

narration.text: Let's walk through the DealState Kotlin data class that models a deal on the ledger. The class is marked with @BelongsToContract linking it to its governing contract so the correct verify logic is applied. It is annotated @CordaSerializable allowing safe serialization when messages cross node boundaries. The data fields include a dealId string, a numeric value, lender and borrower Party objects that represent legal identities, and a status string like PROPOSED, ACCEPTED, or SETTLED. The participants list provides the parties who should receive and interact with this state. A concrete example: when a lender initiates a deal, they create an output DealState with status PROPOSED and participants containing both parties. That ensures both parties see the transaction. A common mistake is omitting a participant; the missing party will not receive the transaction and cannot sign, leading to failing flows. When designing states, keep fields minimal and only include what contracts and flows need to validate and process. Finally, override toString can help debugging during flows and tests but does not affect ledger semantics. How would you change this structure if a regulator needed read-only access while not being a signer?

keyIdea.title: DealState essentials
keyIdea.text: Use @BelongsToContract and participants to link states to contracts and control visibility; include only necessary fields for verification and privacy.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › DealState Kotlin example
What to notice
  • @BelongsToContract ensures this state is validated by the right contract.
  • Party objects represent legal node identities; participants determine distribution.
  • Status strings encode lifecycle stages; transitions are enforced by the contract.
Common mistake

Adding unnecessary sensitive fields increases exposure. Keep participant lists precise to preserve privacy.

Code snippet
@BelongsToContract(DealContract::class)
@CordaSerializable
data class DealState(
  val dealId: String,
  val value: Long,
  val lender: Party,
  val borrower: Party,
  val status: String,
  override val participants: List<Party>
) : ContractState
Example: create output with status PROPOSED and participants list including lender and borrower so both receive the transaction for signing.

screens.title: Contracts and verify()
screens.subtitle: Enforcing business rules before parties sign

narration.text: Contracts are the code that defines the valid transitions of states on the ledger. The central function is verify, which inspects the proposed LedgerTransaction and throws an IllegalArgumentException if any rule is violated. This verify step is executed by each signing party locally before they add their signature. For example, when creating a deal the Create branch in verify can assert that there are no input states, exactly one output, a non-empty deal ID, a positive value, and that lender and borrower are different. Each assertion protects participants from signing an invalid or malicious transaction. A frequent misconception is that the Notary enforces business rules; the Notary's role is to prevent double-spend, not to validate business logic. Therefore robust verify implementations are critical. When composing verify, include clear messages and keep logic deterministic—avoid random numbers or external calls that cause non-deterministic behavior. Also ensure required signers are listed in the command so CollectSignaturesFlow can gather correct keys. A takeaway question: how would you structure verify to allow an Accept command that preserves lender and borrower while changing only status? Contracts and verify() means verify() must assert all preconditions for every command and remain deterministic; parties run verify before signing.. In practical terms, enforcing business rules before parties sign. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Contract rule
keyIdea.text: verify() must assert all preconditions for every command and remain deterministic; parties run verify before signing.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Contracts and verify()
Why verify matters
  • verify prevents invalid state transitions and protects signers.
  • It runs locally for each signer before they sign, so failures abort the flow early.
  • Keep logic deterministic—no randomness or external API calls inside verify.
Misconception
Notary does not validate contract rules. verify is the authoritative check run by signers.
What a verify branch looks like
when (command.value) {
  is DealCommands.Create -> requireThat {
    "No inputs should be consumed when creating a deal." using (tx.inputs.isEmpty())
    "One output state should be created." using (tx.outputs.size == 1)
    val output = tx.outputsOfType<DealState>().single()
    "The deal value must be positive." using (output.value > 0)
  }
  // other branches...
}
Each assertion gives a clear reason so developers and signers can diagnose failures quickly.

screens.title: DealContract.verify: Create, Accept, Settle
screens.subtitle: Step through the assertions that guard transitions

narration.text: Now we'll step through the DealContract. verify implementation that enforces the lifecycle of a DealState. The contract defines three command types: Create, Accept, and Settle. For Create, verify asserts no inputs, exactly one output, a non-empty deal ID, a positive value, distinct lender and borrower, status PROPOSED, and both parties present in participants. This prevents malformed proposals and ensures visibility. For Accept, verify expects one input and one output, matching deal IDs, input status PROPOSED and output status ACCEPTED, unchanged counterparties, and the lender's signature present. Note how the command. signers check ensures only the appropriate party authorizes the transition. For Settle, the contract requires one input, no output, input status ACCEPTED, and both lender and borrower signatures to finalize settlement. A typical misconception arises when developers forget to check signers for specific commands; forgetting this can allow unauthorized state changes. The clear takeaway is that each command branch should check shape, semantics, and signer keys, so signers can trust the transaction before they sign. DealContract.verify: Create, Accept, Settle means each command branch must check structure, semantics, and required signer keys to enforce safe transitions.. In practical terms, step through the assertions that guard transitions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: verify branches
keyIdea.text: Each command branch must check structure, semantics, and required signer keys to enforce safe transitions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › DealContract.verify: Create, Accept, Settle
Verify structure
Each branch performs three checks: the transaction shape (inputs/outputs), semantic assertions (IDs, statuses, values), and signer verification. This prevents malformed or unauthorized transitions.
Create
No inputs, one output, positive value, status PROPOSED, lender != borrower, both participants present.
Accept
One input and one output, IDs match, status moves PROPOSED→ACCEPTED, lender signs.
Settle
One input, no outputs, status ACCEPTED, both lender and borrower sign.
Code excerpt
val command = tx.commands.requireSingleCommand<DealCommands>()
when (command.value) {
  is DealCommands.Create -> requireThat {
    "No inputs should be consumed when creating a deal." using (tx.inputs.isEmpty())
    // other checks...
  }
  is DealCommands.Accept -> requireThat {
    "One input state should be consumed." using (tx.inputs.size == 1)
    // other checks including signer
    "The lender must sign to accept the deal." using (command.signers.contains(input.lender.owningKey))
  }
  // Settle branch...
}
Design verify so failures are descriptive; that helps debugging during flow runs and unit tests.

screens.title: Commands and Signers
screens.subtitle: How commands express intent and list required signers

narration.text: Commands are small instruction objects embedded in transactions that indicate the operation type and encode which keys must sign. For our DealContract we use DealCommands. Create, DealCommands. Accept, and DealCommands. Settle. A Command pairs CommandData with a list of signer public keys. The contract's verify function inspects the Command and asserts that the required signers are present before allowing a transition. For example, when a borrower initiates Accept, the lender's key must appear in command. signers so the lender explicitly authorizes acceptance. Contrast this with including participants on a state, which controls visibility but does not by itself enforce signing. A common error is to omit the appropriate signer from the Command, causing CollectSignaturesFlow to fail to gather the needed keys. Another mistake is listing too many keys, which forces unnecessary approvals. The practical rule: list exactly the keys that must authorize the semantic change and ensure verify checks for those keys. Consider: who should sign a Settle operation for a payment — both parties typically must sign to record finality. Commands and Signers means commands declare intent and required signer keys; verify() must check those keys to enforce authorization.. In practical terms, how commands express intent and list required signers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Command rule
keyIdea.text: Commands declare intent and required signer keys; verify() must check those keys to enforce authorization.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Commands and Signers
Intent vs Authorization
Commands state the intent (Create/Accept/Settle). Signers listed in the command are the keys whose signatures are required to authorize that intent. Verify must confirm these keys are present.
Common mistake
Forgetting to include required signer keys prevents signature collection; including extra keys forces unnecessary approvals.
Concrete example
val command = Command(DealCommands.Accept(), inputDealState.lender.owningKey)
// verify() checks command.signers.contains(input.lender.owningKey)
In Accept, the lender must sign to acknowledge the acceptance. The initiator should list the lender key when building the command, and CollectSignaturesFlow will collect it from the lender's node.

screens.title: Flows: orchestrating a transaction
screens.subtitle: Steps from proposal to final recorded transaction

narration.text: Flows are the executable business processes in Corda that orchestrate the steps required to move states through their lifecycle. A typical initiator flow follows these steps: get a Notary reference, build an output state and command, create a TransactionBuilder, call verify which runs the contract checks, sign the transaction as the initiator, initiate sessions with counterparty nodes, collect their signatures via CollectSignaturesFlow, and finalize using FinalityFlow which submits to the Notary and records the transaction. The responder flow signs after running its own checks in a SignTransactionFlow subclass and then receives the finality notification and records the transaction. For example, in the CreateDealFlow the lender builds a PROPOSED DealState, signs, obtains the borrower's signature, and calls FinalityFlow so both parties record the deal. A common misconception is that flows are only about sending messages; in reality they also build and verify cryptographic state transitions. When designing flows, ensure you handle exceptions and session closures to avoid deadlocks. The key question to reflect on: how does verify's pre-signing execution improve security in this process? Flows: orchestrating a transaction means a flow builds and verifies a transaction, collects signatures with sessions, and finalizes with notarization and recording via finalityflow.. In practical terms, steps from proposal to final recorded transaction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Flow steps
keyIdea.text: A flow builds and verifies a transaction, collects signatures with sessions, and finalizes with notarization and recording via FinalityFlow.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Flows: orchestrating a transaction
Standard flow steps
  1. Get Notary reference.
  2. Build output state and command with required signers.
  3. Create TransactionBuilder and call verify(serviceHub).
  4. Sign initial transaction as initiator.
  5. Initiate sessions and CollectSignaturesFlow.
  6. Call FinalityFlow to notarize and distribute.
Responder flows use SignTransactionFlow to perform checks before signing and ReceiveFinalityFlow to record the finalized transaction.
Flow example card
CreateDealFlow
Builds a PROPOSED DealState, signs, collects borrower signature, finalizes to Notary.
CreateDealResponder
Performs local checks then signs and records final transaction.

narration.text: This walkthrough follows CreateDealFlow, the initiator flow that creates a DealState. First the flow obtains a Notary reference from the network map cache. Then it builds an output DealState including ourIdentity as lender, the borrower party, the value, and status PROPOSED. Next the flow creates a Command of type DealCommands. Create listing all participant keys as signers. The TransactionBuilder is constructed with the notary, the output state, and the command. Calling txBuilder. verify(serviceHub) runs the contract's verify function locally, so any failing assertion aborts before signatures are collected. The initiator signs with signInitialTransaction, then opens a FlowSession with the borrower and calls CollectSignaturesFlow to obtain the borrower's signature. Finally the flow calls FinalityFlow to submit the fully signed transaction to the Notary and distribute and record it at both parties. A misconception to avoid: do not skip verify or assume the Notary checks rules. Verify ensures all parties only sign valid transactions. Reflect: why must the initiator include the required signer keys correctly when building the command? CreateDealFlow walkthrough means call verify before signing, and collect signatures via sessions; finalityflow notarizes and records the transaction for all parties.. In practical terms, build, verify, sign, collect, finalize. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Flow insight
keyIdea.text: Call verify before signing, and collect signatures via sessions; FinalityFlow notarizes and records the transaction for all parties.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › CreateDealFlow walkthrough
Flow outline
  1. Get Notary reference.
  2. Build output DealState with status PROPOSED.
  3. Create Command with participant signers.
  4. Build TransactionBuilder and call verify(serviceHub).
  5. Sign initial transaction and CollectSignaturesFlow with borrower.
  6. Call FinalityFlow to notarize and record.
Handle FlowException and ensure sessions are initiated in the same order in both initiator and responder to avoid deadlocks.
Core code excerpt
val notary = serviceHub.networkMapCache.notaryIdentities.first()
val outputState = DealState(dealId, value, ourIdentity, borrower, "PROPOSED", participants)
val command = Command(DealCommands.Create(), participants.map { it.owningKey })
val txBuilder = TransactionBuilder(notary)
  .addOutputState(outputState, DEAL_CONTRACT_ID)
  .addCommand(command)
// 5. verify
txBuilder.verify(serviceHub)
// 6. sign, collect, finalize...
This sequence ensures contract rules are enforced before any signatures are collected, protecting all parties.

screens.title: Responder flows & AcceptDealFlow template
screens.subtitle: How counterparty checks and Accept flow work

narration.text: Responder flows are how counterparties validate and sign transactions proposed by an initiator. A typical responder uses SignTransactionFlow to implement checkTransaction, which runs local checks on the proposed transaction and only signs if those checks pass. In CreateDealResponder, the borrower confirms they are indeed the borrower in the output DealState before signing. The responder then calls ReceiveFinalityFlow to obtain and record the finalized transaction. The AcceptDealFlow template follows the same pattern but starts with the borrower initiating a flow to accept a PROPOSED deal. AcceptDealFlow retrieves the PROPOSED DealState from the vault by LinearID, builds an output with status ACCEPTED, creates a Command for DealCommands. Accept with the lender's key as required signer, then verifies, signs, collects the lender's signature, and finalizes. The AcceptDealResponder must check that the input status is PROPOSED, the output status is ACCEPTED, and that the responder is the lender before signing. A common pitfall is not filtering by status when querying the vault, which can cause incorrect state selection. The takeaway: responders run local checks and must mirror the contract semantics to avoid signing invalid transactions.

keyIdea.title: Responder insight
keyIdea.text: Responder flows perform local transaction checks and then sign; Accept flows follow retrieve, copy-with-updated-status, command, verify, sign, collect, finalize.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Responder flows & AcceptDealFlow template
Responder pattern
Use SignTransactionFlow and override checkTransaction to enforce local business rules before signing. After signing, call ReceiveFinalityFlow to record the finalized transaction.
Pitfall
Querying the vault without checking status or LinearID can select wrong states; always filter precisely.
AcceptDealFlow snippet
// retrieve PROPOSED DealState by LinearID
val dealStateAndRef = serviceHub.vaultService.queryBy(DealState::class.java)
  .states.filter { it.state.data.linearId == dealLinearId && it.state.data.status == "PROPOSED" }.single()
val input = dealStateAndRef.state.data
val output = input.copy(status = "ACCEPTED")
val command = Command(DealCommands.Accept(), input.lender.owningKey)
// build tx with input and output, verify, sign, collect lender signature, finalize
Responder must check that they are the lender and that status transitions match the contract before signing.

narration.text: Packaging a CorDapp produces a JAR that contains your states, contracts, and flows. For local testing, the standard approach uses Gradle deployNodes which builds node runtimes and places CorDapp JARs into the build/nodes/*/cordapps directories for each test node. For production, JARs are distributed to each node operator to place into their node's cordapps directory before starting the node so the node loads your CorDapp classes at startup. A concrete command for local testing is running./gradlew deployNodes in the project root. Important details: the CorDapp must be compiled against the correct Corda A P I version used by the nodes, and you must not include runtime dependencies that conflict with the node environment. A common deployment mistake is starting nodes without copying the latest JARs into their cordapps folder, which results in nodes running older code. Another pitfall is relying on dynamic behavior in contracts; verify must remain deterministic so all parties can re-run it. After deployment, test flows end-to-end: initiator and responder should both record the same finalized transaction. Reflection: how would you structure release steps to ensure nodes receive coordinated updates without downtime?

keyIdea.title: Deploy rule
keyIdea.text: Use Gradle deployNodes for local testing and distribute CorDapp JARs into each node's cordapps folder for production; ensure API version alignment and deterministic contracts.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Building and deploying CorDapps
Local build
Run the Gradle task to prepare test nodes and place CorDapp JARs into the cordapps folders for each node in build/nodes. Ensure the CorDapp targets the correct Corda API version.
./gradlew deployNodes
Production notes
Distribute the CorDapp JAR to each node operator and place it in their cordapps directory prior to node startup. Avoid including conflicting runtime libraries inside the JAR.
Checklist
  • Confirm Corda API compatibility.
  • Test verify rules with unit tests.
  • Coordinate deployment across nodes to prevent mismatched behavior.

screens.title: Common mistakes & safety notes
screens.subtitle: Pitfalls in states, contracts, flows, and deployment

narration.text: This slide collects the common mistakes you'll encounter when developing CorDapps and how to avoid them. First, an improper participants list is the most frequent source of missing-transaction errors; always include every counterparty that needs to receive or sign. Second, incomplete or incorrect Contract. verify logic leads to failing transactions or worse, incorrect acceptance; write unit tests for every verify branch. Third, flow deadlocks occur when session initiation order or error handling is inconsistent; use clear session ordering and robust exception handling. Fourth, Notary misconfiguration or omission will cause errors—always pick a notary and include it in your TransactionBuilder. Fifth, avoid hardcoding identities; resolve parties using the network map cache or pass Party objects into flows. Sixth, ensure contracts are deterministic—no randomness or external HTTP calls in verify; use oracles when external data is required. Finally, during deployment make sure the node's cordapps directory contains the correct JAR version. For each mistake, the recommended action is a test: unit tests for verify, integration flows for signature collection, and small deploy tests before production rollout. What is the single best test you can write to catch both participant and verify errors early?

keyIdea.title: Safety summary
keyIdea.text: Test participants, contract assertions, flow session ordering, Notary selection, and determinism to avoid common CorDapp failures.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Common mistakes & safety notes
Top pitfalls
  • Missing participants → distribution failures.
  • Uncovered verify() paths → runtime exceptions or insecure transitions.
  • Flow ordering errors → deadlocks or failed signature collection.
  • Notary omitted or misconfigured → transaction errors.
  • Hardcoded identities → brittle, non-portable flows.
Mitigations & tests
Unit test verify branches, integration test end-to-end flows, validate participant propagation from state, and run small node deploy tests with the JAR to confirm runtime behavior.
Pro tip
Write a smoke flow test that creates a deal and checks both parties record the same finalized transaction.

narration.text: Here are three core ideas to remember. First, ContractState models immutable facts; include only the fields necessary for contracts and the participants who must see or sign the transaction. Second, Contract. verify enforces business rules deterministically before signatures are applied; write clear assertions and unit tests for each command branch.
